summary: Defines how SNMP messages are carried over various underlying protocols. It separates the SNMP message format from the transport used to deliver it, so the same messages can travel over different networks. It replaces RFC 1906.

plainLanguage.summary: A letter can go by truck, train or plane. This note says how to put network-management messages onto each kind of delivery service.

questions: what is the minimum snmp message size
subtitle: How SNMP management messages are packed into UDP, OSI, AppleTalk and IPX datagrams.

tldr.problem: SNMP messages need to travel over real networks, but the management protocol itself should not depend on any one network protocol suite.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3417 defines a mapping for each transport: how a message is serialized into one datagram, which well-known values to use, and the smallest message size an entity must accept. All of them use the same Basic Encoding Rules.
tldr.outcome: UDP over IPv4 is the preferred mapping and systems with IPv4 MUST implement it. The RFC replaces RFC 1906 and changes only the editorial text, not the protocol.

today: RFC 3417 is an Internet Standard (STD 62) and obsoletes RFC 1906. It has since been updated by RFC 4789 and RFC 5590.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
SNMP is used to read and change managed objects held in a virtual information store called the Management Information Base (MIB). RFC 3417 describes how the management protocol, whose operations are defined in RFC 3416, may be carried over a variety of protocol suites.

It defines mappings for an initial set of transport domains and says that other mappings may be defined in the future. At the time of writing, work on an IPv6 mapping was in progress, described in RFC 3419.

Although several mappings are defined, UDP over IPv4 is the preferred one. Systems implementing IPv4 MUST implement it, and systems that support other mappings SHOULD also offer access through UDP over IPv4, to maximize interoperability.
sections.plainLanguage: SNMP is a way for a network manager to ask devices questions. This document explains how to put those questions into different kinds of envelopes, and which envelope everyone should be able to open.

sections.title: Transport Domains and Address Formats
sections.content:
Section 2 is a MIB module named SNMPv2-TM. For each transport it defines a transport domain identifier and, for most, a textual convention that says how an address of that kind is laid out as an octet string.

  • UDP over IPv4: SnmpUDPAddress is 6 octets: 4 for the IP address, then 2 for the UDP port, both in network byte order.
  • OSI: SnmpOSIAddress starts with one octet giving the length of the network address (0 or 3 to 20), then the network address, then a transport selector of up to 64 octets. Two domains share it, one for connectionless and one for connection-oriented network service.
  • AppleTalk DDP: SnmpNBPAddress holds an NBP name made of an object, a type and a zone, each a length-prefixed string of up to 32 octets.
  • IPX: SnmpIPXAddress is 12 octets: a 4-octet network number, a 6-octet physical address and a 2-octet socket number.

The module also keeps a deprecated domain for SNMPv1 over UDP over IPv4, used for proxying to SNMPv1.
sections.plainLanguage: Every kind of delivery service writes addresses differently, like street addresses versus post office boxes. This part says exactly how each kind of address is written down.

sections.title: SNMP over UDP over IPv4
sections.content:
This is the preferred mapping. Each message is serialized, using the Basic Encoding Rules, onto a single UDP datagram carried over IPv4. One SNMP message therefore fits in one datagram.

The RFC suggests that administrators configure entities with a command responder application to listen on UDP port 161, and entities with a notification receiver application to listen on UDP port 162.

An entity using this mapping must be able to accept messages of up to and including 484 octets. Accepting messages of up to 1472 octets is recommended, and larger sizes are encouraged whenever possible.
sections.plainLanguage: Each question or answer goes in one small UDP envelope. Devices that answer questions wait at mailbox number 161, and devices that listen for alarms wait at mailbox 162.

sections.title: The Optional Mappings: OSI, AppleTalk and IPX
sections.content:
The other three mappings are optional. Each puts one message into one datagram or transport data unit of that protocol suite.

  • OSI: one message per TSDU of the OSI Connectionless-mode Transport Service. Suggested transport selectors are snmp-l and snmpt-l over a connectionless network service, and snmp-o and snmpt-o over a connection-oriented one. At least 484 octets must be accepted.
  • AppleTalk DDP: DDP protocol type 8, with command responders on socket 8 and notification receivers on socket 9. At least 484 octets must be accepted.
  • IPX: IPX packet type 4. Suggested sockets are 36879 (hex 900f) for command responders and 36880 (hex 9010) for notification receivers. At least 546 octets must be accepted.

AppleTalk nodes are identified by an NBP name rather than an address, because network-level addresses can change at every reboot. The RFC therefore requires nodes to answer NBP lookups and confirms, recommends using NBP lookups sparingly to build a cache of name-to-address mappings, and gives a default minimum cache entry lifetime of 60 seconds.
sections.plainLanguage: There are also envelopes for older networks, such as AppleTalk and IPX. The AppleTalk one is tricky because the devices keep changing street address, so they are found by name and the answers are remembered for a while.

sections.title: Serialization with the Basic Encoding Rules
sections.content:
Every mapping uses the same encoding: the Basic Encoding Rules (BER) for ASN.1, with three restrictions that apply to everything encoded, including message wrappers, PDUs and data objects.

  • Lengths use only the definite form. The indefinite form is prohibited, though extra length octets are allowed in the definite-long form.
  • Simple types (INTEGER, OCTET STRING, OBJECT IDENTIFIER) use the primitive form. The constructed form is used only for structured types such as a SEQUENCE.
  • A BITS value is encoded as an OCTET STRING, with the first named bit in the high-order bit of the first octet. Unused bits of the last octet are zero when sent and ignored on receipt.

The RFC includes a worked example that encodes a GetBulkRequest PDU as hexadecimal, and notes that its outer SEQUENCE deliberately uses more than the minimum number of length octets.
sections.plainLanguage: All the envelopes hold the same kind of letter, written in the same strict code. The code has a few rules so that every device reads it the same way.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC states that SNMPv1 by itself is not a secure environment. Even if the network is secure, for example through IPsec, nothing controls who on that network may read or change the objects behind a command responder.

Implementors are urged to consider the SNMPv3 security features, specifically the User-based Security Model (RFC 3414) and the View-based Access Control Model (RFC 3415). Making sure that only legitimate principals can get or set objects is the responsibility of the customer or user.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone who can reach a device might be able to change its settings unless it is locked properly. So use the newer version of SNMP, which has locks, and set them up carefully.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 1906
sections.content:
RFC 3417 obsoletes RFC 1906. It differs from that document only in editorial improvements, and the protocol is unchanged. The MIB module's revision history traces back through RFC 1906 to an initial version published as RFC 1449.

The IANA considerations are small: the module needs a single object identifier for its module identity, allocated in the snmpModules subtree.
